summary: Describes a dynamic way for IS-IS routers to learn symbolic hostnames, using a TLV that floods each router's name-to-system-ID mapping across the network. This makes logs and commands easier to read than raw system IDs. It obsoleted RFC 2763 and moved the capability onto the standards track. It was updated later by RFC 6232.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS routers identify each other with system IDs, which are difficult to recognize in diagnostic output. This RFC lets a router advertise a symbolic name so other routers can display a readable mapping.

questions: how routers learn names in is-is
what is the is-is dynamic hostname tlv
how do is-is routers learn hostnames
subtitle: How IS-IS routers advertise symbolic names alongside their system IDs.

tldr.problem: IS-IS uses system IDs to identify routers, but operators find symbolic names easier to read in diagnostic output. Static name tables require updates across the network.
tldr.mechanism: A router may include its symbolic name in a Dynamic hostname TLV in an IS-IS link-state PDU. Other routers may use the flooded information to update their name-to-system-ID mappings.
tldr.outcome: The RFC obsoletes RFC 2763 and moves the mechanism to the Standards Track. RFC 6232 later updated it.

today: RFC 5301 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It obsoletes RFC 2763 and has been updated by RFC 6232; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Making Router Diagnostics Readable
sections.content:
IS-IS identifies each node with a system ID that is 1 to 8 bytes long, normally 6 bytes. Operators use these identifiers when checking adjacencies, routing-table entries and the link-state database, but hexadecimal IDs are less readable than symbolic names.

A static table can map names to system IDs and back, but every router needs entries for the whole network. Adding, removing or renaming a router then requires changes on the other routers, making the tables difficult to maintain.
sections.plainLanguage: System IDs identify routers, but names are easier for people to recognize. Maintaining a copy of every name on every router creates repeated configuration work.

sections.title: Advertising Names Through IS-IS
sections.content:
The RFC considers static configuration, DNS and information carried by IS-IS itself. Static tables are hard to keep current. DNS adds a dependency that may be slow or unavailable during network problems, and some implementations may not support the needed records.

The defined mechanism adds a Type-Length-Value (TLV) to IS-IS link-state PDUs. Routers can flood their own name information through the same routing protocol that already distributes network state.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of maintaining distributed tables or relying on DNS, a router can advertise its own name through IS-IS. Other routers receive that information through the routing protocol.

sections.title: The Dynamic Hostname TLV
sections.content:
The Dynamic hostname TLV has type 137. Its value is a string from 1 to 255 bytes and is not null-terminated. The string names the router that originated the link-state PDU; the system ID can be derived from the PDU identifier.

The router may use its fully qualified domain name, part of that name or another operator-chosen string. The RFC strongly recommends using the full name or part of it. The value uses 7-bit ASCII. A user interface that accepts or displays Unicode is responsible for converting it to or from the transmitted format using RFC 3490 algorithms.

The TLV is optional and may appear in any fragment of a non-pseudonode link-state PDU. In a pseudonode PDU, it should not be treated as the router's DNS hostname.
sections.plainLanguage: A router's optional TLV carries a short ASCII name. The receiving router can pair that name with the system ID identified by the link-state PDU.

sections.title: Using an Advertised Name
sections.content:
A router decides whether to include the TLV when it originates a link-state PDU. A receiving router may ignore it or install the name and system ID in its IS-IS hostname-mapping table.

If a received name or system ID differs from the cached mapping, the implementation SHOULD replace the old mapping with the latest information. A router may also use a pseudonode PDU to associate a symbolic name with a local LAN.

The RFC does not require routers to use the TLV. It specifies no new IANA action because the TLV had already been allocated and reserved by RFC 2763.
sections.plainLanguage: Receiving routers may store the advertised name or ignore it. If they store it and receive a changed mapping, they should use the latest information.

sections.title: Security and Trust in Names
sections.content:
The name-to-system-ID mapping comes from routers themselves. A misconfigured or compromised router can therefore advertise false information. The RFC advises treating these mappings cautiously when investigating a suspected security incident.

The mechanism raises no other new security issues for IS-IS. The RFC refers readers to RFC 5304 for IS-IS security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can advertise an incorrect name, whether by mistake or compromise. Do not rely on the mapping alone during a security investigation.
